items.content: Amit opens: 'You come here for enlightenment, but today we will give you intimacy.' The episode was meant to be shot before a live Life…
For years Amit heard Ajay say he'd 'just written a BS article' and admired the extreme modesty. Then he realised BS meant Business…
When Ajay laughs mid-monologue, Amit asks: 'Am I so deeply attractive that you can't just help burst out with happiness?' After Ajay…
Amit's spontaneous-order digression into Gen Z slang: once upon a time it wasn't good to be sick, but 'Today when someone says Amit,…
Explaining prices as a language through which distant strangers fulfil each other's needs and make each other happy, Amit stops himself:…
On the listener who had 'I play to play' tattooed on his arm, Amit was 'obviously very moved', but also couldn't help a 'why body…
Amit's 'vociferous demand': since Ajay preaches generosity, 'you also have to be generous with your fucking recommendations.'
Heading off at the end, Amit tells Ajay to lead 'partly to make sure that any obstacles on the path are encountered by you first and I…
'Know thyself' from the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, cited by Amit as the reason natural selection matters.
Douglas Adams on natural selection, read by Amit: 'I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.'
The Battle of Stalingrad, used by Ajay to show that history only looks inevitable in hindsight and that analogies to it ignore the…
Dan Wang's recent book on China's 'engineer's view of the world', cited by Ajay as the arrogance of believing the world isn't complicated.
Adam Ferguson's phrase for spontaneous order: 'the result of human action, but not human design.'
'A language is a dialect with an army.' Amit uses it to argue that Hindi isn't inherently superior to Bhojpuri or Maithili, and notes…
Max Weber's definition of the state as a community holding a monopoly of physical violence over a territory, which Ajay calls 'the only…
Hanlon's razor ('never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity'), which Amit stretches into: assume the state…
James Buchanan's protective, productive and predatory state. Amit's thesis is that every state eventually morphs into the predatory one.
The Angus Maddison graph of human welfare: flat until the 18th–19th century, then exploding upward. Amit credits the spread of markets…
Raghuram Rajan and Rohini Nilekani's 'state, society, markets' trichotomy, which Amit argued against on his show.
Gorbachev, quoted by Ajay: 'markets are not a feature of capitalism, markets are the invention of civilization.'
Kafkaesque, Ajay's word for being accused without knowing the charge. Rule of law demands a hard document stating the crime and the…
The myth of Sisyphus, reread by Amit as a happy story if the point is rolling the rock, not reaching the top.
Neil Simon, quoted by Amit: 'the world is full of two kinds of people, the watchers and the doers, and the watchers sit around watching…
Annie Dillard: 'How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.'
'Matargashti', which Amit calls 'one of the great terms of our times', and doing it with a friend is his idea of a day well spent.
Dario Amodei's essay title 'Machines of Loving Grace', which Ajay notes is a line from a poem.
